title: Missing Number Problems for Grade 1: A First Taste of Algebra + Free Quiz
meta_title: Missing Number Problems Grade 1 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach missing number problems for Grade 1: the box as an unknown, the balance idea and fact families, with a free 8-question quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: A blank in 7 + __ = 10 is a child’s first algebra problem, whether anyone calls it that or not. Here is how I teach missing-number thinking so it builds real number sense, plus a quick quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write 7 + __ = 10 on a slate and watch what a six-year-old does. Some children freeze, because the blank is not where they expect the answer to be. Others quietly count up from 7 until they hit 10 and whisper ‘three’. That whisper is a big moment, even if nobody in the room calls it by its real name: the child has just solved their first algebra problem. Missing number problems for Grade 1 are exactly that — the earliest, gentlest version of the thinking that becomes x years later.

The mistake I see most often is treating these as ordinary sums with the numbers shuffled around. They are not. A missing-number question asks a child to work backwards from a known result, and that is a genuinely different mental move from ‘what is 7 plus 3’. Get this right in Grade 1 and place value, subtraction and later algebra all get easier. Get it wrong — treat it as guess-and-check — and you build a habit that has to be unpicked later.

What the box actually means

The first thing to teach is that the blank, the box, or the little line is standing in for a number nobody has told us yet. It has one correct value, and our job is to find it. I like to say it out loud to the child: ‘the box is hiding a number — let us catch it.’ Naming the box as a hidden number, rather than an empty space to fill however you like, is the whole game. It is the seed of the idea that a letter can stand for a number.

Keep every example within 20 at this stage. The reasoning is what matters, not big numbers. A child wrestling with 14 + __ = 19 while also struggling to hold 14 in their head is fighting two battles at once.

The balance idea: both sides must match

The equals sign is the most misunderstood symbol in primary maths. Most Grade 1 children read = as ‘the answer comes next’, which is why a question like 6 + 2 = __ + 4 throws them completely — they want to write 8 in the box and move on. So I teach the equals sign as a see-saw, or a taraazu, the two-pan balance every Indian child has seen at a vegetable stall. Whatever weight sits on the left must be matched on the right, or the see-saw tips.

With that picture, 6 + 2 = __ + 4 becomes a fair question. The left pan holds 8. The right pan already has 4, so the box must add 4 more to balance it. The answer is 4, not 8. Children who own the balance idea stop making the classic error, and they carry a correct picture of = all the way to secondary school.

Think addition to subtract

Missing-number subtraction is where fact families earn their keep. Faced with __ − 3 = 5, a child does not need to know any subtraction at all. They can ask the friendlier question: ‘three and what makes… no — what number, take away 3, leaves 5?’ The quickest route is to add back: 5 + 3 = 8, so the box is 8. This is the think-addition-to-subtract strategy, and missing-number problems are the perfect place to build it.

Fact families make four questions from three numbers

The trio 3, 5 and 8 gives a family: 3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 3 = 8, 8 − 3 = 5 and 8 − 5 = 3. A child who sees these four as the same fact from four angles can solve any missing-number problem built on that trio, wherever the blank hides. This is why I drill fact families harder than isolated sums — one family is worth four facts, and it is exactly the flexibility missing-number work demands.

Where the blank hides changes the strategy

The position of the box decides the move. Spend a few minutes sorting problems by type with your child before drilling them; knowing which kind you are looking at is half the solution.

Equation typeExampleHow to solve it
Blank after the sign (result missing)6 + 2 = __Just add. This is an ordinary sum — the easy warm-up.
Blank in an addition7 + __ = 10Count on from 7 to 10, or use the bond: 7 needs 3 to make 10.
Blank as the whole (subtraction)__ − 3 = 5Add back: 5 + 3 = 8. Think addition to subtract.
Blank as a part taken away9 − __ = 4Ask ‘9 take away what leaves 4?’ The gap from 4 to 9 is 5.
Blank with numbers on both sides6 + 2 = __ + 4Balance it: left is 8, right needs 4 more, so the box is 4.

Why this builds number sense, not just answers

Here is the counter-intuitive bit worth holding onto: a child who is slower on missing-number problems but reasons them out is in a far better place than one who races through plain sums. Missing-number work forces flexible thinking — you cannot solve 9 − __ = 4 on autopilot. That flexibility is number sense, and it is what separates children who cope in later maths from those who stall.

  • It rewires the equals sign from ‘answer next’ to ‘both sides balance’ — the single most useful correction you can make in Grade 1.
  • It makes subtraction lean on addition, so a child with shaky subtraction still has a route in.
  • It builds the unknown, so that meeting x in Class 6 feels like an old friend with a new name.
  • It exposes gaps honestly — a child who can do 7 + 3 but not 7 + __ = 10 has memorised a fact without understanding the relationship. Better to find that out now.

A short routine that works

Ten minutes, a few times a week, beats a marathon session. I ask parents to do it in three quick rounds: first a couple of result-missing sums as a warm-up, then two or three addition-blank and subtraction-blank problems, and finally one both-sides balance question to stretch. Say the reasoning aloud together — ‘the box is hiding a number, both sides must match’ — until the child starts saying it back to you. When they narrate their own thinking, you know it has landed.

One honest caveat: do not rush both-sides equations like 6 + 2 = __ + 4. Some children need a term of see-saw talk and physical balancing before it clicks, and pushing early just breeds guessing. Let the balance idea settle first.

quiz.title: Grade 1 Missing Number Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on finding the missing number in addition, subtraction and both-sides-equal equations within 20. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: Count on from 7 to 10, or use the bond to ten: 7 needs 3 more. The box is 3.
Think addition to subtract: add back, 5 + 3 = 8. The whole was 8.
Balance the see-saw. The left pan is 8. The right already has 4, so the box adds 4 more to match.
Ask: 9 take away what leaves 4? The gap from 4 up to 9 is 5, so the box is 5.
What adds to 5 to make 12? Count on from 5 to 12, that is 7. The box is 7.

questions.q: The box is hiding a number. What does the box mean in 4 + __ = 9?
options: The one number that makes it true
questions.explanation: The box stands for the single number that makes both sides equal. Here that number is 5.

questions.q: Which fact helps you solve 8 − __ = 3 fastest?
questions.explanation: The family for 3, 5 and 8 gives 3 + 5 = 8, so 8 take away 5 leaves 3. The box is 5.
The equals sign balances both sides even when the total is on the left. 6 needs 4 more to make 10.

faq.q: Are missing number problems really algebra for a six-year-old?
faq.a: Yes, in the truest sense. Finding the value that makes 7 + __ = 10 true is the same reasoning as solving 7 + x = 10, minus the letter. Grade 1 children handle the idea comfortably when the numbers stay within 20.

faq.q: Why does my child write 8 in 6 + 2 = __ + 4?
faq.a: Because they read the equals sign as ‘the answer comes next’ rather than ‘both sides must match’. Teach = as a see-saw or taraazu that has to balance, and the error usually fixes itself within a couple of weeks.

faq.q: How do I teach subtraction missing numbers like __ − 3 = 5?
faq.a: Use think-addition-to-subtract: add the two known numbers back together. 5 + 3 = 8, so the box is 8. Fact families make this automatic, which is why they are worth drilling more than isolated sums.

Keep everything within 20 in Grade 1. The point is the backwards reasoning, not big arithmetic. Larger numbers just add memory load and hide whether the child actually understands the missing-number idea.
